title: Taking the fraction apart
mystery: Why is one fraction harder than three?
picture: A complicated fraction is several simple ones that were added together — undo the addition.

cards.text: Why is one fraction harder than three?
You can integrate $1/(x-2)$ in your head. You can integrate $1/(x-3)$ in your head. Put them over a common denominator and the result is suddenly a problem you have to think about.

That is the whole technique. The ugly fraction on your exam was assembled from simple ones by somebody adding them together — partial fractions is just running that addition backwards to expose the pieces you already know how to integrate.
A complicated fraction is several simple ones that were added together — undo the addition.

Before decomposing anything, glance at the denominator and name the pieces you expect: distinct linear factors give one term each, a repeated factor earns a term per power, an irreducible quadratic gets a $Cx+D$ on top.
